newsitem.title: CHINA: China official brushes aside concerns on Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: China official brushes aside concerns on Hong Kong.

text.p: China's top policy maker for Hong Kong on Wednesday brushed aside concerns about a businessman heading the territory's government after 1997 but said the candidate would not be able to use the post for personal gain.

"You cannot use the position for the benefit of a group or an individual," Lu Ping, head of the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office of China's State Council (cabinet), told a business conference in Beijing.

"It is not a question of whether it is a businessman (heading the government)," he said in reply to a question raised by another Hong Kong-based businessman about just such a possible conflict of interest.
"It is a matter of character, fairness and not seeking personal gain."
The chief executive will replace Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten when Britain hands back the territory to Chinese rule on July 1, 1997, after 150 years of colonial rule.
A group of 400 people -- all of them carefully screened by Beijing -- will choose the post-handover chief executive next month, and two of the top candidates are from the business community.
Some people in the territory have voiced concern that a businessman would put narrow commercial interests ahead of those of the territory as a whole.
Shipping tycoon Tung Chee-hwa, who stepped down from the Orient Overseas (International) shipping group in October, is one of the leading candidates.

Peter Woo, now in public service, is also from the colony's business sector though he has severed active links to the two public arms of the shipping empire of his late father-in-law, Sir Yue-kong Pao.
Two other candidates are former chief justice Ti Liang Yang and retired judge Simon Li.
